title: Beijing’s Next Play for the South China Sea
gist: Brookings' Lynn Kuok argues China has shifted from high-intensity maritime clashes to a quieter gray-zone campaign — flag raisings on unoccupied features like Sandy Cay, a nature reserve at Scarborough Shoal, floating structures, and a massive new reclamation at Antelope Reef set to become its largest South China Sea outpost — designed to normalize control below the threshold that triggers a response. She warns that the Iran war's energy and remittance shock plus U.S. tariffs are pushing even the Philippines toward accommodation with Beijing, which would gut Washington's exposure-based strategy.

themes.theme: Shift from Sea Rights to Land Features

insights.claim: Chinese coast guard personnel unfurled the Chinese flag on Sandy Cay, an uninhabited Spratly sandbar, in April 2025 — China's first formal on-the-ground assertion of sovereignty over an unoccupied land feature in more than a decade.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Marks a regime change in Chinese tactics from contesting rights at sea to contesting territory itself — a new and less legally answerable escalation channel.
insights.locator: In April 2025, Chinese coast guard personnel stepped onto Sandy Cay

insights.claim: By targeting uninhabited features, Beijing is straining the 2002 nonbinding ASEAN Declaration on the Conduct of Parties commitment to self-restraint from inhabiting unoccupied features, a norm claimant states had respected for almost a quarter of a century.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
entities: Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea
insights.so_what: Erosion of the one restraint that has kept the Spratlys frozen — its collapse invites copycat occupations by other claimants.
insights.locator: For almost a quarter of a century, claimant states fortified features

insights.claim: Sandy Cay lies barely two nautical miles from Philippine-occupied Thitu Island, so their 12-nautical-mile territorial seas overlap almost entirely, meaning a Chinese claim to Sandy Cay narrows Philippine operational space and lays groundwork to legally challenge Philippine patrols around a major outpost.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Shows how a symbolic flag planting converts into concrete legal leverage over an adversary's existing base — the mechanism to watch elsewhere.
insights.locator: The Sandy Cay landing involved only a Chinese flag

insights.claim: Because sovereignty over land features remains unresolved — unlike sovereign rights over water, which the Hague tribunal clarified — most Chinese moves on land fall into a legal gray zone, giving governments far fewer clear legal grounds to challenge them than they have at sea.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
entities: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea
insights.so_what: Explains why the land campaign is deliberately chosen: it neutralizes the legal toolkit that has been the West's main instrument of pushback.
insights.locator: China maintains it is free to act on features

themes.theme: Antelope Reef and the New Island-Building Campaign

insights.claim: China began large-scale dredging in October 2025 to expand Antelope Reef in the Paracels, roughly 215 nautical miles east of the central Vietnamese coast, in its first significant island-building campaign in about a decade.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: A decade-long pause in reclamation has ended — expect renewed regional militarization headlines and Vietnamese security recalibration.
insights.locator: In October 2025, China began large-scale dredging

insights.claim: Satellite imagery indicates Antelope Reef is on track to become China's largest military outpost in the South China Sea, with the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative assessing it could host a runway, harbor, missile facilities, underground storage, and surveillance and electronic warfare systems.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
entities: Center for Strategic and International Studies
insights.so_what: Extends Chinese sensing and strike coverage toward Vietnam and adds redundancy for naval and air operations — a material shift in the regional military balance.
insights.locator: Satellite imagery suggests the reef is on track

insights.claim: China's 2013-2015 campaign only enlarged seven features it already occupied, whereas the current phase extends activity to features it does not hold, marking a qualitative rather than merely quantitative escalation.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: The distinction between fortifying held features and seizing unheld ones is the escalation threshold investors and policymakers should track.
insights.locator: Between late 2013 and 2015, when the bulk of that work

insights.claim: If China occupied and militarized Scarborough Shoal, that base combined with the Paracel and Spratly outposts would extend Chinese sensor and strike reach toward the Luzon Strait between the Philippines and Taiwan and place Manila well within striking range.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Ties South China Sea creep directly to Taiwan contingency planning — Scarborough militarization would be a step-change in regional risk pricing.
insights.locator: If China were to occupy and militarize Scarborough Shoal

themes.theme: Gray-Zone Playbook: Salami Tactics Below the Response Threshold

insights.claim: High-intensity Chinese incidents — military-grade lasers, water cannons, ramming and dangerous maneuvers used frequently between February 2023 and July 2024 — became less common, replaced by marine scientific research, symbolic sovereignty assertions and temporary floating structures near disputed features.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Falling incident counts are a tactical substitution, not de-escalation — headline-driven risk models will understate the trend.
insights.locator: Beijing’s methods have been shifting, too

insights.claim: Individually inconsequential Chinese acts can collectively alter the strategic landscape because coastal states judge each single move too minor to justify a response that risks escalation.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: A general salami-slicing model applicable beyond the South China Sea: the defender's escalation-aversion is the attacker's operating margin.
insights.quote: Individually, China’s quieter acts might seem inconsequential. Collectively, they could alter the strategic landscape.
insights.locator: Individually, China’s quieter acts might seem inconsequential

insights.claim: Washington's response to the Sandy Cay flag raising was merely that reports of a Chinese seizure were 'deeply concerning if true,' and it made no public response at all to the Antelope Reef reclamation, while it did join Manila in rejecting the Scarborough nature reserve.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Evidence that the gray-zone approach is working — inconsistent U.S. responses lower the expected cost of each incremental Chinese move.
insights.locator: The Sandy Cay episode elicited only a minor response

insights.claim: Beijing's September 2025 approval of a national nature reserve at Scarborough Shoal — a feature it has controlled access to since 2012 without occupying — lets it assert jurisdiction and recast fishing restrictions as environmental law enforcement.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Environmental regulation as a sovereignty instrument is a replicable and hard-to-oppose technique — watch for similar designations at other features.
insights.locator: China has also sought to consolidate its administrative control

insights.claim: China's aim in both the maritime and land domains is the steady accumulation of advantage rather than a single decisive victory, betting that gray-zone tactics can gradually normalize its control across the South China Sea.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Rules out a single dramatic trigger event — the risk is a slow reset of the regional order that markets never price on any given day.
insights.quote: the steady accumulation of advantage rather than a single decisive victory
insights.locator: After a decade in which Chinese pressure focused

themes.theme: Offshore Energy as the Recurring Flash Point

insights.claim: Beijing has repeatedly targeted offshore energy activity — warning Hanoi against drilling in Vietnam's exclusive economic zone in 2017 and 2018, triggering a months-long Vanguard Bank standoff with a survey vessel in 2019, and shadowing the West Capella drillship contracted by Malaysia's state energy company for weeks in 2020.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Southeast Asian offshore E&P carries a persistent, demonstrated interference risk that raises the cost of capital for blocks inside contested EEZs.
insights.locator: Offshore energy sites became recurring flash points

insights.claim: China maintains a presence around Reed Bank, a submerged atoll the Hague tribunal placed within the Philippine exclusive economic zone and continental shelf, where Manila is pursuing energy development, and conducted an unauthorized survey there in May.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Reed Bank is the specific asset where Philippine gas development and Chinese pressure collide — the test case for any joint-development deal.
insights.locator: China also maintains a presence around Reed Bank

insights.claim: Chinese research vessels are increasingly operating in the Philippine exclusive economic zone without coast guard or maritime militia escorts and typically withdraw when challenged, according to Philippine authorities.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Unescorted survey ships are the low-cost, deniable vanguard of the campaign — their movements are a leading indicator of where Beijing acts next.
insights.locator: Philippine officials say that Beijing is making greater use of research vessels

themes.theme: Legal Architecture and the Hague Ruling's Limits

insights.claim: The Hague tribunal's ruling a decade ago rejected any Chinese historic-rights claim within the nine-dash line — a demarcation for which Beijing has never provided coordinates — and found that no Spratly feature, Scarborough Shoal or Reed Bank generates an exclusive economic zone.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: The legal baseline is settled and favorable to claimants at sea, which is precisely why Beijing has shifted the contest to unresolved land sovereignty.
insights.locator: Ten years ago, a tribunal in The Hague

insights.claim: China rejected the tribunal ruling but temporarily paused its most obviously inconsistent conduct — interfering with neighbors' resource rights and driving non-Chinese fishermen from Scarborough Shoal — and resumed once international attention waned.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Chinese restraint is a function of sustained international attention, not law — attention decay is the reliable predictor of renewed pressure.
insights.locator: China immediately rejected the decision but paused conduct

insights.claim: The BRP Sierra Madre, deliberately grounded at Second Thomas Shoal in 1999 and still in commission with Philippine marines aboard, means an armed attack on the ship or its personnel could invoke U.S. commitments under the 1951 U.S.-Philippine Mutual Defense Treaty.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: The single clearest automatic tripwire for U.S.-China armed confrontation in the region — resupply-mission incidents deserve outsized attention.
insights.locator: In 1999, Manila had deliberately grounded a Philippine naval vessel

insights.claim: A July 2024 provisional arrangement between Manila and Beijing allowed 13 resupply and rotation missions to proceed without untoward incidents as of March, but the two sides disagree about the arrangement's scope and Chinese coast guard personnel struck a Filipino sailor with a wooden baton in a recent encounter.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: The de-escalation arrangement is fragile and undefined — a scope dispute is the most likely path back to a treaty-triggering incident.
insights.locator: Chinese attempts to block these missions have resulted

insights.claim: Renewed pressure on land could kill the prospects for a South China Sea Code of Conduct, and even though a final deal is unlikely, the polite fiction that the parties are near one has itself afforded some stability.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Diplomatic theater has real stabilizing value — the visible collapse of Code of Conduct talks would itself be a risk event.
insights.locator: All this could further weaken the prospects for a Code of Conduct

themes.theme: Philippine Vulnerability to the Iran War and U.S. Tariffs

insights.claim: The Philippines sources roughly 98 percent of its crude oil imports from the Middle East and about 2.4 million of the three million Southeast Asians living or working in that region are Filipinos, making it among the Southeast Asian states hardest hit by the Iran war's economic fallout.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: A direct transmission channel from Gulf conflict to Philippine fuel costs and remittance flows — and therefore to Manila's willingness to confront Beijing.
insights.quote: It sources roughly 98 percent of its crude oil imports from the Middle East.
insights.locator: Within Southeast Asia, it is among the hardest hit

insights.claim: President Marcos said in March that the Iran war could provide the impetus for an agreement with Beijing on oil and gas development, and days later his government restarted high-level talks with China on energy cooperation and maritime de-escalation.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: An energy shock is actively converting into geopolitical realignment — Philippines-China joint development is now a live scenario to monitor.
insights.quote: the Iran war could provide the “impetus” for an agreement with Beijing on oil and gas development
insights.locator: In March, he said that the Iran war could provide

insights.claim: Marcos faces domestic pressure after corruption-related failures in flood-control infrastructure contributed to hundreds of deaths in 2025, compounding tariff and energy strains and constraining his room to take a hard line with Beijing.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Domestic political weakness, not strategic preference, is the variable most likely to soften Philippine resistance to China.
insights.locator: Disruptions to energy supplies and uncertainty over remittance flows

insights.claim: Previous Philippine-China energy talks collapsed in 2018 and 2019 over Philippine constitutional constraints and Beijing's refusal to acknowledge Philippine sovereign rights in any final agreement, and the same obstacles plus deep public and defense-establishment suspicion still apply.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Joint development headlines should be discounted — the binding constraint is constitutional, not political, and has never been resolved.
insights.locator: Still, energy cooperation between China and the Philippines remains fraught

insights.claim: Severe external shocks — the Iran war and U.S. tariffs — plus domestic political strains may make some form of Southeast Asian rapprochement with Beijing increasingly difficult to avoid even for states determined to curb China's worst impulses.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: U.S. tariff policy is directly undermining U.S. security alignment in Southeast Asia — a second-order cost rarely counted in trade analysis.
insights.locator: Southeast Asian states determined to curb China’s worst impulses

themes.theme: U.S. Strategy: Coast Guard, Credibility and the Exposure Trap

insights.claim: Washington's regional strategy depends on publicly exposing Beijing's unlawful conduct to rally allies, so if Manila steps back from its 'radical transparency' policy and highly visible clashes, the United States will find it harder to mobilize coordinated responses to China in the South China Sea and beyond.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: The core second-order risk: a quiet Philippine rapprochement would disarm the main U.S. coalition-building tool across the Indo-Pacific.
insights.locator: A Philippine adjustment along these lines could make it harder

insights.claim: U.S. support for Manila now includes a $336 million military modernization carve-out from the broader foreign aid freeze, congressional authorization of up to $2.5 billion in grants through 2030 for U.S.-made defense equipment, and a $60 million grant program approved in June to modernize the Philippine energy sector.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: A concrete multi-year procurement pipeline for U.S. defense exporters, plus energy-sector aid explicitly framed as reducing Chinese leverage over Manila.
insights.locator: U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth visited Manila

insights.claim: Countering China's gray-zone strategy requires more than conventional naval power because the U.S. Coast Guard is better suited to law-enforcement-style encounters and can respond to Chinese coast guard and maritime militia vessels with less escalation risk than a naval deployment.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Implies a shift in the relevant capability mix toward cutters, patrol vessels and maritime domain awareness rather than blue-water combatants.
insights.quote: Countering this strategy requires more than conventional naval power.
insights.locator: Countering this strategy requires more than conventional naval power

insights.claim: Washington and Manila should agree in advance to a graduated diplomatic, economic and operational response to any Chinese attempt to reclaim and establish a permanent outpost at Scarborough Shoal, the author's single highest priority.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: Names the specific red line whose crossing would trigger the region's next major crisis — a discrete, observable escalation marker.
insights.locator: A particular priority is preventing Beijing from reclaiming

insights.claim: Even Philippine-Japanese negotiations to delimit overlapping exclusive economic zones as required under the law of the sea drew Chinese denunciation and coast guard 'law enforcement patrols' asserting sovereignty over Taiwan and its maritime rights, showing that lawful cooperation itself now carries costs.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
entities: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea
insights.so_what: Beijing is extending deterrence to routine legal diplomacy, and explicitly linking South China Sea patrols to its Taiwan claim.
insights.locator: Manila and Tokyo have also recently announced negotiations

insights.claim: Effective pushback depends on U.S. credibility — regional states must trust Washington to act dependably, counter China without needless escalation, and observe the international law it invokes — which requires correcting policies that constrain partners' ability to resist Beijing.
insights.speaker: Lynn Kuok
insights.so_what: An implicit critique of tariff and aid-freeze policies: economic coercion of partners directly degrades the security coalition against China.
insights.locator: These efforts depend on Washington’s credibility
